value.mechanism: Execution occurs inside a restricted environment with controlled resources and host-facing operations.
value.effect: Reduces the ability of failures and vulnerabilities to spread.
value.conditions: Strength depends on enforcement of the sandbox boundary.

value.mechanism: Network, host inspection, input devices and other resources are disallowed or heavily restricted.
value.effect: Limits the guest's ability to harm the host.

value.mechanism: System-call filtering is one of the Linux kernel mechanisms used for application sandboxing.

value.mechanism: A virtual machine emulates a complete host computer so a conventional guest OS can boot and run.

value.conditions: Host-resource access is mediated through the emulator.

value.mechanism: Host resources are accessed through the emulator rather than natively.
Network-access restrictions and a restricted filesystem namespace define the jail boundary.

value.mechanism: Predetermined rules govern process spawning, code injection, network use and file/registry access.

value.mechanism: A sandbox mimics or replicates a target desktop and contains malware execution.
value.effect: Researchers can evaluate malware behavior without exposing the real target host.
value.conditions: A nonrepresentative environment may not reproduce target behavior.

value.mechanism: Only read(), write(), exit(), and sigreturn() are permitted.
value.conditions: The allowlist is exactly as stated in the source.

value.mechanism: The HTML5 sandbox attribute restricts iframe content.
value.effect: Embedded content runs under a constrained browser context.
value.inverse_or_converse: Removing the attribute removes those restrictions.

value.label: 1996 — Secure Environment for Untrusted Helper Applications
Sandbox vs virtualization
value.description: Sandboxing is a security mechanism; virtualization can provide a highly controlled environment but is broader.

value.label: Restricted OS vs full VM
value.description: A restricted process environment is distinct from a VM emulating a complete host computer.

value.label: Kernel mechanism vs policy
value.description: seccomp/cgroups/namespaces are listed Linux building blocks; rule-based frameworks impose access policy.

value.label: Android UID isolation
value.description: The described Android sandbox uses per-application Linux user IDs.

value.label: Jail vs VM
value.description: A jail is characterized by network and filesystem namespace restrictions rather than full hardware emulation.

value.label: Capabilities vs rules
value.description: Capabilities grant rights through tokens; rule-based systems assign access levels through rules.

value.label: OS vs instruction isolation
value.description: SFI constrains native instructions to memory segments.

value.label: Defense vs analysis
value.description: Sandboxing can contain threats and provide a controlled observation environment.

value.label: Restriction vs absolute denial
value.description: Resources may be disallowed or heavily restricted; sandboxing is not necessarily total denial.

value.label: Guest vs host
value.description: The sandbox boundary separates guest execution from host resources.

value.label: Security mechanism vs application container
value.description: The source presents sandboxing as a security mechanism and does not equate it with application containerization.

value.label: Trusted vs untrusted code
value.description: Sandboxing is especially useful for unverified/untrusted code.

value.label: Browser active code vs unrestricted code
value.description: Native Client and iframe sandboxing show active browser code can execute under restrictions.

value.label: Strict vs normal syscall surface
value.description: Strict seccomp exposes only four named system calls.

value.label: Embedded vs top-level content
value.description: HTML5 sandbox specifically constrains iframe content.

value.label: Platform-specific mechanisms
value.description: Linux, Android, Apple, Windows, browser and language runtimes use different mechanisms.

value.label: Virtual-hosting jail
value.description: Jails are noted as common in virtual hosting.

value.label: Fine-grained capability control
value.description: Capability systems are explicitly described as fine-grained sandboxing.

Online judges and pastebins are explicit non-malware use cases.

The source characterizes jails through network and filesystem namespace restrictions.
Tokens/capabilities grant specific rights; rule systems assign access levels.
The source includes browser, runtime, capability and instruction-level mechanisms.
SFI isolates specified native-code instruction effects into memory segments.

source_claims.statement: Sandbox separates running programs to mitigate spread of system failures and software vulnerabilities.
Sandbox resources include storage and memory scratch space; network access, host inspection and input-device access are usually restricted.
Sandboxing can be comparable to virtualization when providing a highly controlled environment.
Sandboxing is implemented by executing software in a restricted operating-system environment.
Linux application sandboxing uses seccomp, cgroups and namespaces.
Android assigns each application its own Linux user ID for application sandboxing.
GrapheneOS hardens app sandboxing and allows sandboxing every app as described.
Apple App Sandbox is required for specified App Store apps and recommended for other signed apps.
Virtual machines emulate a complete host computer and mediate host-resource access through the emulator.
Jails restrict network access and filesystem namespace and are common in virtual hosting.
Rule-based execution controls process spawning, code injection, network access and file/registry operations.
Security researchers use sandboxing to analyze malware behavior in replicated target environments.
Google Native Client sandboxes compiled C/C++ code in browsers independently of the user's OS.
Capability systems use opaque tokens to grant specific rights and can operate at kernel or user-space levels.
Strict seccomp permits only read, write, exit and sigreturn.
HTML5 iframe sandboxing restricts embedded content.
Java virtual machines sandbox untrusted applets/code.
.NET CLR Code Access Security restricts untrusted code.
SFI isolates store, read and jump assembly instructions into memory segments.
Online judges and executable pastebins are sandbox use cases.

source_claims.text: System image is a serialized copy of entire computer-system state in non-volatile form.
Disk cloning can produce a system image only when relevant state is on disk; some state may be outside disks or inaccessible.
Exact shutdown/restoration capability makes system images usable as backups.
Hibernation images the computer's entire RAM.
Process image captures process state and creates persistence.
DBMS can dump database state before closing and restore it after restart.
Emulators may save system images called savestates in video gaming.
Mobile agents can migrate by saving, copying, and restarting state elsewhere.
Smalltalk and Lisp support system images; Lisp can preserve compiled/customized code and loaded data.
Executable images can be distributed to avoid repeated initialization.
Lisp Machines boot from Worlds containing OS, applications, and data; incremental Worlds store changes.
System images resemble core dumps structurally but have different purposes.

value.name: Four-layer model
value.expression: Application → Transport → Internet → Link
value.meaning: Functional TCP/IP decomposition.

value.name: Encapsulation
value.expression: application data → transport unit → IP datagram → link frame → medium
value.meaning: Data gains protocol context while descending the stack.

value.name: Decapsulation
value.expression: medium → frame → IP datagram → transport data → application
value.meaning: Receiver reverses encapsulation.

value.name: IP forwarding
value.expression: destination IP → routing decision → next hop → repeated forwarding → destination
value.meaning: IP moves datagrams across networks.

value.name: TCP reliability
value.expression: connection + ordering + retransmission + flow control + congestion control
value.meaning: TCP supplies reliable transport over IP.

value.name: UDP service
value.expression: application data → UDP datagram → IP → link
value.meaning: UDP provides connectionless best-effort transport.

value.name: Endpoint addressing
value.expression: IP address + transport port → application endpoint
value.meaning: Host location plus service/channel identity.

value.name: IPv4 to IPv6
value.expression: 32-bit IPv4 → exhaustion → 128-bit IPv6
value.meaning: Address-space expansion.

value.name: End-to-end architecture
value.expression: simple forwarding core + intelligent endpoints
value.meaning: Core forwards; endpoints provide broader intelligence/reliability.

value.name: TCP/IP and OSI mapping
value.expression: TCP/IP application≈OSI session+presentation+application; transport≈transport; internet≈network; link≈data-link/physical boundary
value.meaning: Approximate cross-model correspondence.

value.name: HTTP/3 stack
value.expression: HTTP/3 → QUIC → UDP → IP → Link
value.meaning: Modern HTTP/3 transport chain.

value.name: NFS example stack
value.expression: NFS → XDR → RPC → UDP → IP → Link
value.meaning: Source example demonstrating cross-layer composition.

value.distinction: TCP/IP is an Internet architecture; OSI is a seven-layer general reference model.
IP provides internetworking; TCP provides reliable transport.
TCP is connection-oriented/reliable; UDP is connectionless/best-effort.
IP addresses identify hosts/locations; ports identify service channels.
IP packets are carried inside local link frames.
Layering defines scopes; encapsulation wraps data across those scopes.
End-to-end concerns endpoint intelligence; layering concerns functional separation.
IPv6 expands addresses from 32 to 128 bits.
Gateway was an earlier term for router.
QUIC is a transport protocol carried by UDP.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC exclusively.
User protocols serve applications; support protocols serve infrastructure.
IP/UDP provide best-effort while TCP/SCTP can provide reliability.
TCP/IP link/physical correspondence varies by representation.
IETF routing protocols carried over IP can be categorized as application-layer protocols in the cited TCP/IP treatment.

value.misconception: TCP/IP has seven layers exactly like OSI.
value.correction: TCP/IP's standard four-layer representation differs from OSI.

value.misconception: IP guarantees reliable delivery.
value.correction: IP is best-effort; reliability can be added above it.

value.misconception: TCP and IP are the same protocol.
value.correction: TCP is transport; IP is internetworking.

value.misconception: UDP has no error detection.
value.correction: UDP uses a checksum for error detection.

value.misconception: A port is another IP address.
value.correction: A port identifies a logical communication channel/service.

value.misconception: Routers normally interpret application payloads.
value.correction: Routers generally forward encapsulated traffic without application interpretation.

value.misconception: TCP/IP defines a mandatory separate physical layer.
value.correction: Physical details may be implicit below the link layer.

value.misconception: HTTP/3 runs over TCP.
value.correction: HTTP/3 works exclusively through QUIC, which is carried over UDP.

value.misconception: IPv6 is just a faster IPv4.
value.correction: The source emphasizes IPv6's expanded 128-bit addressing to address exhaustion.

value.misconception: End-to-end means there are no middleboxes.
value.correction: The source explicitly notes firewalls, NATs and caches changed the original assumption.

source_claims.claim: TCP/IP organizes communication into four functional layers and specifies packetization, addressing, transmission, routing and reception.
IETF maintains the suite's technical standards and the suite predates OSI.
DARPA-sponsored ARPANET research and BBN IMPs formed early infrastructure.
Kahn and Cerf hid differences among local networks and delegated reliability to hosts.
The 1978 reformulation separated TCP and IP into distinct transport and internetwork functions.
End-to-end design, encapsulation and layering are central architectural principles.
IPv4/TCP-IP became active on ARPANET in 1983 and DoD standardized TCP/IP for military networking.
Transport provides channels, ports, reliability, segmentation, flow/congestion control and multiple protocol choices.
Application protocols include both user and support protocols and usually treat lower layers as abstractions.
TCP/IP and OSI use different layer representations and IETF does not require strict OSI compliance.
TCP/IP is hardware independent and has implementations across essentially every computing platform.
Minimal implementations include IP, ARP, ICMP, TCP, UDP and IGMP; IPv6 adds NDP and ICMPv6 among its support protocols.

value.name: System VM abstraction
value.expression: Physical hardware -> Hypervisor -> isolated Guest VM -> Guest OS
value.meaning: System virtualization substitutes for a real machine and permits an entire OS to execute in an isolated environment.

value.name: Process VM abstraction
value.expression: Host OS -> Process VM -> Program
value.meaning: A process VM runs as a normal host application and abstracts the underlying hardware/OS for one process.

value.name: OS-level virtualization model
value.expression: Shared kernel + isolated resource views + resource limits -> isolated OS environments
value.meaning: OS-level virtualization partitions resources through the kernel while guest environments share the host OS kernel.

value.name: Snapshot restore model
value.expression: VM state(t_snapshot) + overlays_after_snapshot -> discard overlays -> restored state
value.meaning: Restoring a snapshot disregards changes made after the snapshot point and redirects new changes to a new overlay.

value.name: Migration model
value.expression: VM snapshot/state + target hypervisor -> resumed VM on target host
value.meaning: A VM can be stopped/snapshotted/moved/resumed on another host; synchronized snapshots can reduce interruption.

value.name: Failover model
value.expression: Host failure + last coherent backup state -> VM continuation
value.meaning: Failover continues VM operation from the last-known coherent state available to the backup server.

value.name: Nested virtualization model
value.expression: Outer hypervisor -> VM -> nested hypervisor -> nested guest VM
value.meaning: Nested virtualization recursively places hypervisors/VMs inside another virtualization layer.

value.name: Process VM lifecycle
value.expression: Process start -> VM creation; process close -> VM deletion
value.meaning: The process VM exists for the lifetime of its associated process.

value.name: Same-page memory sharing
value.expression: Identical read-only VM pages -> one physical page
value.meaning: KSM can merge identical pages to improve physical-memory efficiency.

value.name: Full virtualization condition
value.expression: Simulated hardware sufficient for unmodified guest OS
value.meaning: Full virtualization permits an unmodified guest OS designed for the same instruction set to run in isolation.

value.name: System VM vs Process VM
value.description: System VM provides a whole machine/guest OS abstraction; process VM supports a program/process abstraction.

value.name: Host vs Guest
value.description: Host is the physical machine; guest is the virtual environment executing on it.

value.name: Full vs Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
value.description: Full virtualization describes the guest-facing virtualization behavior; hardware-assisted virtualization describes architectural support that facilitates the VMM.

value.name: System VM vs OS-level Virtualization
value.description: System VM can execute a complete guest OS; OS-level environments share the host OS kernel.

value.name: VM vs Virtual Memory
value.description: Virtual memory abstracts memory; system virtualization generalizes machine abstraction and can include privileged instruction handling.

value.name: Snapshot vs Backup
value.description: Snapshot is a point-in-time VM state; failover may use backup-server material representing a last coherent state.

value.name: Migration vs Failover
value.description: Migration deliberately moves a VM to another host; failover continues after host failure using last-known coherent state.

value.name: Namespace-style isolation vs VM isolation
value.description: OS-level virtualization shares a kernel; system VMs isolate through separate guest environments.

value.name: Process VM vs Interpreter
value.description: A process VM is the runtime abstraction; an interpreter is one implementation mechanism.

value.name: JIT vs Interpreter
value.description: JIT is an optimization/compilation technique that can improve process-VM performance; interpreter is an execution mechanism.

value.name: Nested vs ordinary virtualization
value.description: Nested virtualization places a hypervisor inside another hypervisor; ordinary system virtualization does not require recursive layers.

value.name: KSM vs memory overcommitment
value.description: KSM merges identical pages; memory overcommitment is the broader memory-sharing/resource-management context.

value.name: Virtual disk vs snapshot overlay
value.description: Virtual disk is the VM storage abstraction; overlay is a snapshot layer storing subsequent changes.

value.name: Guest OS vs host OS
value.description: Guest OS executes inside VM; host OS is the surrounding OS when applicable.

value.name: Isolation vs Portability
value.description: Isolation separates execution environments; process VMs use abstraction to provide platform independence.

value.misconception: A virtual machine always means a full guest operating system.
value.correction: Process VMs execute a single program/process and can exist entirely as a host-OS application.

value.misconception: System VMs and process VMs are the same abstraction.
value.correction: They operate at different abstraction levels: whole-machine/OS versus program/process.

value.misconception: OS-level virtualization creates a separate kernel for every guest.
value.correction: The source says OS-level guest environments share the host OS kernel.

value.misconception: Full virtualization requires modifying the guest OS.
value.correction: The source defines full virtualization as sufficient simulated hardware for an unmodified guest OS.

value.misconception: Hardware-assisted virtualization is the same thing as full virtualization.
value.correction: Hardware assistance describes architectural support for the VMM; full virtualization describes the guest-visible virtualization model.

value.misconception: A snapshot is just a backup copy of one disk file.
value.correction: Snapshots can include VM storage and other state such as RAM, BIOS and configuration.

value.misconception: Migration and failover are identical.
value.correction: Migration intentionally moves state; failover responds to host failure from last coherent backup state.

value.misconception: Nested virtualization means running containers inside containers.
value.correction: The source defines it as running VMs/hypervisors inside another virtualization layer.

value.misconception: Process VMs cannot use JIT compilation.
value.correction: The source explicitly identifies JIT as an implementation/performance technique for process VMs.

value.misconception: VMs always hide distributed communication in cluster environments.
value.correction: The source states cluster-oriented process VMs do not hide that communication takes place.

value.misconception: KSM and memory overcommitment are identical.
value.correction: KSM is a specific page-merging mechanism within broader memory sharing/overcommitment.

value.misconception: Docker is unrelated to virtualization.
value.correction: The source explicitly classifies Docker as an OS-level virtualization example.

value.core_problem: Provide abstractions that let software execute as though it has a dedicated computer or portable execution environment while sharing physical computing resources.
value.central_model: Physical hardware -> virtualization layer -> isolated system VM/guest OS OR host OS -> process VM -> portable program.
value.central_insight: Virtual machines are not one single mechanism. source_claims.claim: A VM virtualizes or emulates a computer system; system VMs execute whole OSs while process VMs execute programs in platform-independent environments.
System VM architecture includes host/guest terminology, historical time-sharing motivations, memory sharing, embedded uses, sandboxing and server consolidation.
Process VMs are host applications supporting one process and provide platform-independent programming environments; cluster-oriented variants abstract communication.
VM history spans 1960s time-sharing, IBM systems, compiler intermediate representations, p-code, Smalltalk, JIT, Self, HotSpot and register-based VMs.
Full virtualization and hardware-assisted virtualization are distinct techniques with IBM, Intel and AMD historical milestones and many implementation examples.
OS-level virtualization partitions resources through the kernel, shares the host OS kernel and includes Docker and container technologies.
Snapshots capture VM state/storage; overlays form a coherent virtual disk; migration moves VM state; failover uses last-known coherent backup state.
Nested virtualization recursively runs hypervisors/VMs and may rely on hardware support such as VMCS shadowing.
VMs are used for security isolation and compartmentalization architectures can limit malware spread.

misconceptions.correction: Snapshots can include VM storage and other state such as RAM, BIOS and configuration.

misconceptions.misconception: Migration and failover are identical.
misconceptions.correction: Migration intentionally moves state; failover responds to host failure from last coherent backup state.

misconceptions.misconception: Nested virtualization means running containers inside containers.
misconceptions.correction: The source defines it as running VMs/hypervisors inside another virtualization layer.

misconceptions.misconception: Process VMs cannot use JIT compilation.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly identifies JIT as an implementation/performance technique for process VMs.

misconceptions.misconception: VMs always hide distributed communication in cluster environments.
misconceptions.correction: The source states cluster-oriented process VMs do not hide that communication takes place.

misconceptions.misconception: KSM and memory overcommitment are identical.
misconceptions.correction: KSM is a specific page-merging mechanism within broader memory sharing/overcommitment.

misconceptions.misconception: Docker is unrelated to virtualization.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly classifies Docker as an OS-level virtualization example.

why_it_matters.central_model: Physical hardware -> virtualization layer -> isolated system VM/guest OS OR host OS -> process VM -> portable program.

value.misconception: A volume is always a physical disk.
value.correction: A volume is logical and may be partition-based, span media, or be packed in a file.

value.misconception: Every partition is automatically a usable volume.
value.correction: An OS can recognize a partition without recognizing its volume filesystem.

value.misconception: An ISO volume is a partition.
value.correction: The source treats an ISO9660 volume image as a file in a host volume, not a partition.

value.misconception: Windows and Unix-like systems expose volumes the same way.
value.correction: Windows uses drive letters/NTFS mount points; Unix-like systems graft volumes into a filesystem tree.

value.misconception: Moving a file always copies its data.
value.correction: Within one volume the move can be metadata-only; across volumes content must be copied.

value.misconception: A volume label is a permanent unique identifier.
value.correction: Labels are user-assignable; serial numbers provide a more fixed identifier.

value.misconception: Relabeling and formatting have the same identity effect.
value.correction: Formatting typically changes the serial; relabeling does not.

value.misconception: A volume has exactly one path.
value.correction: The source allows multiple path forms, including multiple drive letters via SUBST.

value.misconception: A drive letter identifies physical hardware directly.
value.correction: A drive letter identifies a logical volume in the OS namespace.

value.misconception: FAT, NTFS and exFAT use identical label constraints.
value.correction: The source gives different limits and character behavior for each.

source_claims.title: Definition
source_claims.statement: A volume or logical drive is a distinctly-addressable storage area with a single file system.

source_claims.title: Storage topology
source_claims.statement: Mass storage is commonly divided into partitions used as volumes; volumes may span multiple media for redundancy, while simple volumes use one medium without redundancy or striping.

source_claims.title: Windows example
source_claims.statement: The source's two-drive example maps D0/P0 to NTFS C:, D0/P1 to FAT32 D:, and D1/P0 to FAT32 E:.

source_claims.title: Partition versus volume recognition
source_claims.statement: An OS may recognize a partition without recognizing its volume when it is unformatted or uses an unsupported filesystem such as ext4 in the Windows example.

source_claims.title: File-packed volume
source_claims.statement: A volume can be packed in one file, such as an ISO9660 disc image or Apple Disk Image; because it is a file inside a host volume, it is not a partition.

source_claims.title: Windows mounting
source_claims.statement: Windows handles volumes in the kernel and configures volumes/mount points through Disk Management or diskpart; mounted volumes receive paths via drive letters or NTFS mount points.

source_claims.title: Unix mounting
source_claims.statement: Unix-like systems commonly use volume managers and mount; non-boot volumes are grafted into the filesystem tree at a mount point.

source_claims.title: Cross-volume performance
source_claims.statement: Moving a file within a volume can change metadata without copying content, while moving across volumes requires copying content and deleting the source.

source_claims.title: Identifiers
source_claims.statement: Volumes can use human-readable labels and more fixed identifiers; serial numbers historically originated on mainframes and later supported media-change detection.

source_claims.title: FAT/NTFS labels and serials
source_claims.statement: FAT, NTFS, and exFAT impose different volume-label constraints; FAT/NTFS serial numbers support detection of volume replacement and formatting changes the serial.
